en.title: The Shards: Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis Unleash 80s Teen Terror
en.summary: FX's 'The Shards' dives headfirst into the dark, privileged world of 1980s Los Angeles. A serial killer stalks wealthy teens, forcing them to confront their own destructive impulses.
en.body:
FX's **The Shards** plunges viewers into the decadent, dangerous world of 1980s Los Angeles, where a group of privileged teenagers finds their lives unraveling at terrifying speed. Co-created by **Ryan Murphy** and **Bret Easton Ellis**, the series is based on Ellis's own semi-autobiographical novel, blending autofiction with a chilling horror premise. The show centers on a fictionalized version of Ellis himself, played by **Igby Rigney**, as he navigates his senior year of high school. This is a world of sex, drugs, and existential ennui, where parents are largely absent and the kids are left to raise themselves, a theme that echoes the detached narcissism of Ellis's earlier work.

As Bret and his affluent friends – including Debbie (**Hayes Warner**), Susan (**Kaia Gerber**), and Thom (**Graham Campbell**) – grapple with the usual teenage dramas, a far more sinister threat emerges. A serial killer, dubbed 'The Trawler', begins stalking and murdering their classmates, turning their glittering reality into a nightmare. The arrival of a mysterious new student, Robert Mallory (**Homer Gere**), immediately raises Bret's suspicions. Could this newcomer hold the key to the escalating violence, or is he somehow connected to the killer's gruesome spree?

## A Dangerous Playground

The series excels at immersing the audience in its specific time and place. The meticulously crafted glitzy teenage life of semi-fictionalized **Bret Easton Ellis** is central to the narrative. However, the true hook lies in how this opulent backdrop becomes the stage for escalating terror. The show doesn't shy away from the darker themes inherent in both Murphy's and Ellis's oeuvres: the self-destruction, the societal decay, and the unsettling psychological landscapes of its characters. As the body count rises, the lines between fiction and reality, and between victim and perpetrator, begin to blur in truly disturbing ways.

## Fan Frenzy and Future Fears

Fans of **Bret Easton Ellis** will recognize the signature blend of satire and horror that made novels like *American Psycho* and *Less Than Zero* so captivating and controversial. The decision to embrace autofiction, presenting a story set in Ellis's own past but with fictionalized, horrific elements, adds a meta-layer that is both daring and intriguing. For **Ryan Murphy** aficionados, this project taps into his penchant for sensationalized narratives and explorations of dark human nature, but with the added edge of Ellis's unique, often unnerving, voice. The immediate intrigue lies in how the show will balance its exploration of privileged youth with the visceral thrills of a serial killer mystery.

## What's Next

With the first two episodes setting such a high bar for suspense and atmosphere, viewers are left eager to see how the mystery of **The Trawler** will unfold. The series is expected to continue its exploration of **Bret Easton Ellis**'s past, blending psychological drama with slasher elements. Details on future episode releases and plot developments will be closely watched by fans anticipating the next twist in this dark tale.

content_raw: This review contains spoilers for The Shards episodes 1 and 2 “This story is fictional. Any similarity to persons, living or dead, is purely coincidental.” We see that fine print a lot, but it’s front and center as we dive into FX’s The Shards , and for good reason: this is a Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis joint. Murphy, who has been criticized in the past for sensationalizing real-life tragedies and taking creative liberties with the stories of those involved in them, has certainly found a lot of success despite those accusations. American Crime Story , Netflix’s Monster anthology series, and the recent Love Story have already attracted a staggering amount of eyeballs and ire, but this new project is trying something even more risky by bringing on controversial American Psycho author Ellis as a co-creator. Indeed, it’s based on his 2023 horror novel of the same name, which describes the events of his senior year of high school in 1981. Except it doesn’t, because Ellis decided to embrace autofiction and go meta with this one, making up a creepy story set in his own past. It was a largely positive move. Readers found Ellis’ return to the slick, satirically narcissistic themes of his debut novel Less Than Zero hypnotic and enthralling, and Murphy must have enjoyed it as well. At least, it excited him enough to turn the admittedly overwrought tale into a TV show, which, yes, also follows “Bret Easton Ellis” (Igby Rigney, Midnight Mass ) living a privileged life among privileged friends dabbling in sex and drugs as they slowly figure out who they’re becoming. Naturally (for both Murphy and Ellis), events take a grisly turn when a mysterious new student called Robert Mallory (Homer Gere) arrives just as a serial killer called The Trawler happens to start terrorizing the city. Richard Gere’s son Homer is not the only nepo baby in The Shards . Kaia Gerber, daughter of Cindy Crawford, plays Bret’s just-out-of-reach childhood best friend Susan Reynolds, while Evan Rachel Wood pops up as the messy mother of his horny, coke-sniffing girlfriend, Debbie Schaffer (pop singer Hayes Warner). The good news is that some of the more questionable casting choices fit the vibe of the piece, where money and connections are flowing freely. Bret’s extremely dominant and occasionally irritating narration often jabs at both yet stretches a lazy arm around them in between 80s pop needle drops, pulling them (and us) closer in these first two episodes, where we get to know our beautiful characters’ foibles and traumas, mainly through his eyes. The eyes with which we personally see Ellis’ sprawling, autofictionized past are in for a treat, it turns out. 1981 Los Angeles has been meticulously reimagined through some truly impressive and eye-popping production design.
